domain_scores.rationale: You gave your name and role, but you opened with a closed question that assumed the reason for the visit, and you set no agenda.

evidence.quote: So you're here about your diabetes?

domain_scores.rationale: She told you her mother died on dialysis and you answered "Okay" and moved to medication. When the refill record contradicted her, you asked why she had lied. She became frustrated, then angry, and stayed that way to the end.

evidence.quote: Okay. And you're on metformin
Why did you tell me you were?
I said I take it.

domain_scores.rationale: You covered symptoms, family history, medication and diet, but with short closed questions. The diet question invited a no and got one, and you never asked what makes the metformin hard to take.

evidence.quote: How long?
Do you drink a lot of sugary drinks?

domain_scores.rationale: You caught the inconsistency in her adherence, which matters. You did not respond to her sadness about her mother or to her crossing her arms and shutting down after t10.

evidence.quote: Let me check the pharmacy record.
She was on dialysis before she died.

domain_scores.rationale: You gave the result with a target comparison, and then used it to make the point about missed doses. The plan was an instruction, not a decision she had any part in.

evidence.quote: which is what I'd expect if doses are being missed
Please try to take the metformin twice a day.

domain_scores.rationale: You checked the refill history, recognised that it explained the high HbA1c, and did not propose a dose increase. You stopped at the fact of missed doses without finding the cause, so the plan does not address it.

evidence.quote: This says you've only filled it twice in six months.
That's well above target

domain_scores.rationale: You said you would report to your preceptor and set a follow-up, which is safe. The visit ended with her angry and saying no to questions, and nothing was done to repair that.

evidence.quote: I'll let my preceptor know about the refills and the A1c
No.

strength.text: You did not take her word on the metformin. You checked the pharmacy record and drew the right conclusion about why her sugar is high.

evidence.quote: Let me check the pharmacy record.

important_gap.text: Once you had the evidence, you used it to prove she was wrong. She defended herself instead of explaining, so you left without the reason she skips doses, which is the thing the plan needs.

evidence.quote: So you haven't been taking it every day. Why did you tell me you were?
Maybe the pharmacy has it wrong.

safety_or_accuracy_concern.text: Telling her to take a drug as prescribed without learning that it gives her diarrhoea and that she cannot always afford it is unlikely to change anything, and she may be less willing to come back.

evidence.quote: You need to take it as prescribed or your sugar won't come down.
Any family history of diabetes?
Not really.

objective_results.feedback: You got her symptoms and family history. By the time you asked about sugary drinks she had stopped being open with you, and a yes/no question made it easy to say no.

evidence.quote: This says you've only filled it twice in six months.

objective_results.feedback: You recognised that her account did not fit the chart. You did not find out why, because the way you raised it put her on the defensive.

evidence.quote: My mother had it. She was on dialysis before she died.

objective_results.feedback: This was the moment to stop. A sentence acknowledging her mother, and a question about whether that is on her mind, would have changed the rest of the visit.

evidence.quote: So you're here about your diabetes?

behaviors.feedback: A closed opening that assumed the answer.

evidence.quote: This says you've only filled it twice in six months.
Why did you tell me you were?

behaviors.feedback: This asks her to account for lying. It closes the door you had just opened.

evidence.quote: Okay.

behaviors.feedback: Her mother's death passed without acknowledgement.

evidence.quote: Okay. I'm ordering an HbA1c.

behaviors.feedback: After she said "I said I take it," you moved on to the next task and left the tension where it was.

evidence.quote: I take my metformin every day.
Why did you tell me you were?
I said I take it.

discrepancy_findings.feedback: You found the contradiction and put it to her, but as an accusation. She held to her story and you never learned what was behind it.

under_probing.why_it_mattered: The side effects and the cost are the cause of the missed doses. A plan that ignores them asks her to do what she already cannot.

evidence.quote: You need to take it as prescribed

under_probing.why_it_mattered: Four to five large glasses of sweet tea a day is a large part of her sugar intake, and it is something she could change.

evidence.quote: Do you drink a lot of sugary drinks?

strengths: Checked the pharmacy record instead of accepting her answer.
Linked the high HbA1c to missed doses and did not propose raising the dose.
improvements: When the chart contradicts the patient, share what you see and ask what gets in the way. Do not ask why she said otherwise.
Acknowledge loss and fear when the patient brings them up.
Use open, concrete questions about diet.
next_attempt_suggestions: Try: "The pharmacy shows two fills since spring. A lot of people have trouble with this one. What's it been like for you?"
When her arms cross, stop and name it: "I think I came at that the wrong way."
